Empirical Research Plan  
“Corporate Governance, Product-Market Competition, and Firm Performance, 1990-2006”

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
Strategy chosen: Difference-in-Differences with a Triple–Difference (DDD) extension.  

Why DID/DDD?  
•  The 2002 Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) – specifically the Section 404 internal-control provisions that became effective for “accelerated filers” (public float ≥ $75 million) in fiscal years ending after 15 Nov 2004 – forced a sharp, externally imposed improvement in several governance dimensions (board/audit-committee independence, internal-control certification, whistle-blower channels, etc.).  
•  Firms below the $75 m float cutoff (“non-accelerated filers”) were exempt until 2007, giving us a clean treatment vs. control split that is plausibly unrelated to unobserved future performance.  
•  By interacting this exogenous governance shock with pre-existing industry-level competition, we obtain a DDD estimator of the causal impact of better governance when product-market competition is high vs. low.  
•  Annual Compustat coverage, 1990-2006, delivers a long pre-trend window, lets us run event-study graphs, and allows the inclusion of rich firm and year fixed effects.

Formal estimating equation (baseline):

Perf_it = β₀ + β₁ (Post_t × Large_i)  
             + β₂ (Post_t × Large_i × HighComp_it)  
             + β₃ Controls_it + μ_i + λ_t + ε_it           (1)

β₂ is the triple-diff coefficient of interest; μ_i are firm FEs and λ_t year FEs.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control

Treatment variable  
• Treat_i,t = 1 if firm i is an “accelerated filer” (public float ≥ $75 m measured in 2001) and year t ≥ 2004 (first fiscal year subject to Section 404).  
• Governance quality G_it (e.g., BoardInd_it, G-Index_it) should jump for treated firms after 2004.

Control group  
• Firms with public float < $75 m (non-accelerated filers) over the same period.

Treatment timing  
• Event year = 2004. We use –5 ≤ τ ≤ +5 event-time windows for event-study graphs.

Competition split  
• HighComp_it = 1 if firm-i’s industry-year HHI_t is below the pooled-sample median (equivalently, above-median competition).  
  – Sensitivity checks: use Lerner Index and Boone Indicator.

No RDD running variable is used; the cutoff fuels the DID.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions

A1. Parallel trends (size groups).  
  Absent SOX, performance gaps between large and small firms would have evolved similarly within the same competition group. Plausible because Section 404 threshold is mechanical; validated with pre-trend event studies.

A2. No anticipation.  
  Firms could not fully implement costly Section 404 controls before the compliance deadline. Board/audit-committee changes were phased-in but largely ex-post 2003.

A3. No spillovers/SUTVA.  
  Governance changes in large firms do not directly alter the potential outcomes of small firms in the same industry (plausible; governance is firm-specific).

A4. Exogeneity of the $75 m float threshold.  
  Public float measured in 2001 is predetermined with respect to 2004–06 outcomes.

A5. Stable composition.  
  Treatment and control samples remain in Compustat; we will verify no differential delistings.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation

T1. Differential size-related shocks unrelated to governance (e.g., access to credit after 2001).  
 • Mitigation: Add firm-specific linear size trends; control for log(Assets), leverage, industry-year FEs.

T2. Measurement error in competition indices or governance quality.  
 • Mitigation: Use multiple competition proxies; instrument governance change with Section 404 as an additional first-stage where governance is the endogenous regressor.  

T3. Concurrent regulations that differentially hit large firms (e.g., Reg FD, NYSE rules).  
 • Mitigation: Include year×industry FEs; show placebo tests around other cutoffs ($50 m, $100 m) to demonstrate specificity; re-estimate after dropping 2002-03 transition years.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)

```r
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional FE regressions
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
df <- read_csv("compustat_1990_2006.csv")

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    # governance proxies
    board_ind      = bd_indep,          # board independence %
    g_index        = g_index,           # G-Index (lower = stronger governance)
    # firm performance
    roa            = oibdp / at,        # return on assets
    tobins_q       = (at + mkvalt - ceq) / at,
    # treatment indicators
    large          = as.integer(public_float_2001 >= 75),   # pre-determined
    post           = as.integer(year >= 2004),
    treat          = large * post,
    # competition
    hhi_ind        = hhi,                               # already in data
    highcomp       = as.integer(hhi_ind < median(hhi_ind, na.rm = TRUE)),
    # triple diff
    ddd            = large * post * highcomp,
    firm_id        = gvkey
  )

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main regression (DDD)
model_ddd <- feols(
  roa ~ treat + ddd + large:highcomp + post:highcomp |
        firm_id + year,
  cluster = ~firm_id,
  data = df
)
summary(model_ddd)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-study pre-trend check
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(event_year = year - 2004)

model_event <- feols(
  roa ~ i(event_year, large, ref = -1) | firm_id + year,
  cluster = ~firm_id,
  data = df %>% filter(event_year >= -5, event_year <= 5)
)
iplot(model_event)          # visually inspect parallel trends

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: alternative competition metric
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(lerner = (sales - cogs) / sales,
         hi_comp_alt = as.integer(lerner < median(lerner, na.rm = TRUE)),
         ddd_alt = large * post * hi_comp_alt)

model_alt <- feols(
  roa ~ large*post + ddd_alt |
        firm_id + year,
  cluster = ~firm_id,
  data = df
)
summary(model_alt)
```

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results

Economic theory (monitoring vs. competition as substitute complements) usually predicts that strong governance is more valuable when external discipline from the product market is low (i.e., low competition).  
However, Section 404 improvements mainly curb managerial slack; in highly competitive markets slack is costlier, so better governance SHOULD translate into higher efficiency exactly where competition is high.  

Prior: β₂ > 0.  
Magnitude: +0.4–0.8 pp increase in ROA (roughly 6–12 % of the 1990-2006 mean ROA) and a 5–8 % increase in Tobin’s Q for treated–high-comp firms relative to controls.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID method)

C1: Parallel pre-trends visually and statistically confirmed ………………… 1  
C2: No spillovers / SUTVA plausible …………………………………………………… 1  
C3: No anticipation / manipulation around $75 m cutoff …………………… 0.8 (~1)  
C4: Stable composition (no selective delisting) …………………………………… 0.8  
C5: No other contemporaneous shocks differentially affecting groups … 0.6  

Overall score ≈ 4.2 / 5 → the design is reasonably strong but hinges on careful pre-trend validation and robustness checks.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
